basic_information.name: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
basic_information.creator: Anthropic (announced November 25, 2024; donated to Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation in December 2025, co-founded with Block and OpenAI)
basic_information.release_date: November 25, 2024 (public announcement and initial specification release)
basic_information.license: MIT License (Python SDK) | Apache License 2.0 for new contributions / MIT for existing code (TypeScript SDK). The specification itself is open-source under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation.
basic_information.current_version: Specification: 2025-11-25 (latest stable release). Python SDK: v1.26.0 (released January 24, 2026). TypeScript SDK: v1.26.0 (released February 5, 2026). Stable v2 SDK anticipated Q1 2026.

technical_architecture.architecture_pattern: protocol | event_driven — MCP is not a framework or agent runtime but an open protocol specification. It follows a client-host-server architecture using JSON-RPC 2.0 as the wire format. The Host process coordinates multiple Client instances, each maintaining a 1:1 connection with an MCP Server. Servers expose three primitive types: Tools (executable functions), Resources (data/context), and Prompts (reusable templates). The protocol is transport-agnostic with defined transports for stdio (local) and Streamable HTTP (remote, replacing older HTTP+SSE). Designed as a universal 'USB-C for AI' — a single standard interface for connecting any AI model to any external system.
technical_architecture.underlying_models: Model-agnostic by design. MCP is a protocol, not tied to any specific LLM. Adopted by: Anthropic Claude (Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Claude API), OpenAI (ChatGPT Desktop, Agents SDK, Responses API), Google (Gemini, Agent Development Kit), Microsoft (Copilot, VS Code, GitHub Copilot), and hundreds of other AI products. Any LLM with tool-calling capabilities can use MCP through client implementations. SDKs available in Python, TypeScript, Java, Kotlin, C#, Swift, Go, and Rust.
technical_architecture.tool_integration: MCP IS the tool integration protocol. Servers expose tools via a standardized JSON schema interface. Three primitive types: (1) Tools — model-controlled functions with JSON Schema input validation and structured output, (2) Resources — application-controlled data sources (files, databases, APIs) that provide context to the model, (3) Prompts — user-controlled reusable templates and workflows. Tools support annotations for read-only vs. destructive operations, cost estimation, and open-world interaction hints. The official registry (registry.modelcontextprotocol.io) provides a community-driven directory for discovering MCP servers.
technical_architecture.planning_approach: Not applicable — MCP is a protocol, not an agent framework. It does not implement planning. Planning is handled by the LLM or agent framework using MCP. The protocol provides the tool/resource/prompt interface that planning systems consume. MCP's contribution to planning is making tools universally discoverable and consistently described so any planning approach (ReAct, tree-of-thought, graph-based) can use them.
technical_architecture.multi_agent_support: MCP enables multi-agent architectures but does not prescribe them. A single Host can manage multiple Clients connected to multiple Servers. The 2025-11-25 spec introduces 'Sampling with Tools' (SEP-1577), allowing MCP servers to initiate sampling requests with tool definitions included, enabling server-side agent loops. MCP is complementary to Google's A2A (Agent-to-Agent) protocol — MCP handles agent-to-tool communication while A2A handles agent-to-agent communication. The Agentic AI Foundation governs both MCP and related standards.

memory_and_context.memory_types_supported: none (protocol-level) — MCP is a stateless protocol; it does not manage memory itself. The 2025-11-25 specification introduced stateless operation modes and async Tasks. Memory management is the responsibility of the Host/Client application or the agent framework using MCP. MCP Resources can serve as external memory sources (connecting to vector stores, databases, knowledge bases), but the protocol itself does not maintain state between sessions.
memory_and_context.context_window_management: Not applicable at protocol level. MCP provides Resources as a mechanism for clients to fetch relevant context from external sources, effectively enabling retrieval-augmented context management. The protocol supports pagination for large resource responses. Context window management is handled by the Host application or agent framework, not by MCP itself.
memory_and_context.persistence_mechanism: Stateless by design (2025-11-25 spec). The protocol supports both stateful (session-based) and stateless operation modes. For stateful mode, session IDs are used to maintain connection context. The async Tasks feature (experimental) provides 'call-now, fetch-later' semantics where task handles persist across requests. Actual persistence of conversation or agent state is handled by the application layer.
memory_and_context.context_engineering_approach: MCP treats context as a first-class architectural concern at the protocol level through its Resources primitive. Resources provide structured access to external context (files, databases, APIs, knowledge bases) with standardized discovery, reading, and subscription mechanisms. This enables systematic context engineering: applications can dynamically discover and retrieve relevant context from multiple sources through a unified interface. The protocol's three primitives map to different context control levels: Resources (application-controlled context), Prompts (user-controlled context templates), and Tools (model-controlled actions).

capabilities.core_capabilities: Universal protocol for connecting AI models to external tools and data. Three core primitives: Tools (executable functions for LLMs), Resources (structured data/context sources), and Prompts (reusable interaction templates). JSON-RPC 2.0 wire format with transport-agnostic design. Two standard transports: stdio (local, process-based) and Streamable HTTP (remote, bidirectional, replaces deprecated HTTP+SSE). OAuth 2.1 authorization framework with PKCE, Client ID Metadata Documents (CIMD), enterprise-managed authorization, and step-up authorization flows. Async Tasks (experimental) for long-running operations with status polling. Elicitation (URL mode) for secure browser-based user interactions (OAuth, payments, API keys). Sampling with Tools for server-initiated LLM requests enabling server-side agent loops. Tool annotations for metadata (read-only, destructive, cost hints). Resource subscriptions for real-time updates. Server-to-client notifications. Capability negotiation during initialization. Official community-driven registry for server discovery. MCP Apps Extension (SEP-1865, November 2025) for UI embedding in AI chatbots, co-developed by Anthropic and OpenAI.
capabilities.supported_modalities: Text, code, structured data (JSON), files, database queries, API calls, web content, browser automation. The protocol itself is modality-agnostic — it transports JSON-RPC messages. Actual modality support depends on the MCP servers connected: filesystem servers handle files, browser servers handle web content, database servers handle SQL, etc. Not inherently limited to any modality.
capabilities.autonomy_level: Not applicable — MCP is a protocol, not an agent. The protocol provides the infrastructure for any autonomy level. Tool annotations (read-only vs. destructive) enable clients to implement appropriate approval workflows. The specification recommends that implementations require user consent for sensitive operations. Autonomy decisions are made by the Host application.
capabilities.tool_ecosystem: 8,240+ MCP servers listed on PulseMCP (as of early 2026). 10,000+ active public MCP servers reported across all registries. Official reference servers maintained by MCP steering group at github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers (50,000+ GitHub stars by May 2025). Categories include: developer tools (GitHub, GitLab, Jira, Linear), databases (PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Redis, Neo4j), cloud services (AWS, GCP, Azure), productivity (Notion, Slack, Google Drive, Asana), browser automation, file systems, web search, and more. Official MCP Registry at registry.modelcontextprotocol.io launched September 2025 with API freeze v0.1 in October 2025. Third-party directories: PulseMCP, mcpservers.org, mcp.so, mcp-awesome.com (1,200+ quality-verified).

agent_interoperability.mcp_support: MCP IS the protocol. It defines the standard for agent-to-tool interoperability. All MCP-compatible clients can connect to all MCP-compatible servers, creating a universal tool ecosystem.
agent_interoperability.a2a_support: MCP and A2A (Google's Agent-to-Agent Protocol) are complementary, not competing. MCP handles agent-to-tool communication; A2A handles agent-to-agent communication. Both are governed under related open-source foundations. The AAIF (governing MCP) and A2A ecosystem are expected to converge. A practical architecture layers both: MCP for tool access, A2A for multi-agent orchestration.
agent_interoperability.agents_md_support: AGENTS.md is a sibling project under the same Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF). AGENTS.md was contributed by OpenAI as a founding project alongside MCP (contributed by Anthropic) and goose (contributed by Block). The two standards are designed to work together: AGENTS.md provides project-specific instructions for coding agents, while MCP provides the tool/data connectivity layer.
agent_interoperability.cross_framework_compatibility: Extremely high — MCP is the de facto industry standard for AI tool integration. Adopted by virtually every major AI product and framework: Anthropic Claude (Desktop, Code, API), OpenAI (ChatGPT, Agents SDK, Codex), Google (Gemini, ADK), Microsoft (Copilot, VS Code, GitHub Copilot), Cursor, Windsurf, Replit, Sourcegraph, JetBrains, Zed, and many more. All major agent frameworks support MCP: LangChain/LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen, smolagents, AWS Strands Agents, Google ADK. SDKs available in 8+ programming languages. The protocol's adoption across competitors (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Microsoft) is unprecedented in the AI industry.

safety_and_guardrails.permission_model: capability_based | sandbox — The specification recommends principle of least privilege: MCP servers should be launched with restricted access to file system, network, and system resources, with users explicitly granting additional privileges as needed. Tool annotations classify operations as read-only or destructive. OAuth 2.1 authorization with PKCE for remote server authentication. Step-up authorization enables runtime escalation when operations require additional permissions. However, the permission model has been criticized as insufficient: local MCP servers can execute arbitrary code, and the spec's sandboxing recommendations are not enforced at the protocol level.
safety_and_guardrails.escalation_policy: The protocol supports user consent flows via Elicitation (URL mode), which redirects users to browser-based authorization when additional permissions are needed. Step-up authorization (2025-11-25 spec) handles cases where a server needs elevated privileges during an operation. Tool annotations help clients decide which operations require human approval. Actual escalation implementation is left to the Host application.
safety_and_guardrails.hallucination_mitigation: Not directly addressed at protocol level — MCP is a transport protocol, not an inference system. However, MCP Resources enable grounding LLM responses in authoritative data sources, which is a key anti-hallucination strategy. The protocol's structured tool interface with JSON Schema validation ensures well-formed inputs and outputs. Hallucination mitigation remains the responsibility of the client/agent framework.
safety_and_guardrails.audit_trail: Yes — the JSON-RPC 2.0 message format provides structured, parseable records of all tool invocations, resource reads, and server responses. Implementations can log all protocol messages. OpenTelemetry integration is supported for distributed tracing. The protocol supports request/response correlation via JSON-RPC IDs. Multiple observability platforms (Datadog, Langfuse, Moesif, SigNoz) provide MCP-specific monitoring and audit capabilities.
safety_and_guardrails.human_oversight_pattern: pre-approval | confidence_threshold — Tool annotations (read-only vs. destructive) enable clients to implement tiered approval: allow read-only operations automatically while requiring approval for destructive ones. Elicitation redirects sensitive operations (payments, credential entry) to browser-based user flows. The specification explicitly states that implementations should require user consent for sensitive operations. However, the protocol does not enforce any specific human oversight pattern — it provides the metadata and mechanisms for clients to implement their chosen pattern.

governance_and_standards.governance_body: Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF), a directed fund under the Linux Foundation (established December 9, 2025). Platinum members: Amazon Web Services, Anthropic, Block, Bloomberg, Cloudflare, Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI. The AAIF Governing Board handles strategic investments, budget allocation, member recruitment, and project approval. Individual projects like MCP maintain full autonomy over technical direction. Previously governed solely by Anthropic from November 2024 to December 2025.
governance_and_standards.contributing_protocols: MCP itself is the protocol. It is the primary project of the AAIF alongside AGENTS.md (OpenAI) and goose (Block). The protocol builds on established standards: JSON-RPC 2.0 (wire format), OAuth 2.1 with PKCE (authorization), HTTP/SSE (transport), RFC 9728 (Protected Resource Metadata). The MCP Apps Extension (SEP-1865) was co-developed by Anthropic and OpenAI for UI embedding. The protocol is designed to be complementary to Google's A2A protocol for agent-to-agent communication.
governance_and_standards.regulatory_compliance: No direct regulatory compliance certifications for the protocol itself — MCP is a specification, not a deployed service. Compliance depends on the implementation. The specification includes security best practices, authorization framework (OAuth 2.1), and data handling guidelines. Enterprise-managed authorization supports integration with corporate identity providers (SSO, IdP). GDPR and data sovereignty considerations are implementation-dependent. The donation to the Linux Foundation signals maturity for enterprise adoption. MCP gateways (Stacklok, Solo.io, Pomerium) provide enterprise security layers including audit logging and policy enforcement. [uncertain]

deployment_and_operations.deployment_modes: local | cloud | hybrid | edge — MCP servers can run anywhere: (1) Local via stdio transport (subprocess on the same machine as the Host), (2) Remote via Streamable HTTP transport (cloud-hosted, containerized), (3) Serverless (AWS Lambda, Cloud Run — ideal for stateless tools), (4) Kubernetes (enterprise-scale with horizontal scaling), (5) Edge deployments possible for lightweight servers. AWS provides official guidance for deploying MCP servers on AWS (ECS, Lambda, API Gateway). Docker containers are the standard deployment unit for remote servers.
deployment_and_operations.scalability_model: horizontal | serverless — MCP servers are independent processes that scale independently. Each server handles one concern (single-responsibility). Horizontal scaling via container orchestration (Kubernetes), load balancers (HAProxy, cloud-native LBs). Serverless deployment scales to zero and auto-scales based on demand. The protocol's stateless mode (2025-11-25) enables easier horizontal scaling. MCP gateways provide centralized routing, caching, and load distribution.
deployment_and_operations.cost_per_task: The protocol itself is free (open-source). MCP server hosting costs vary: (1) Local stdio servers: zero incremental cost (run on user's machine), (2) Cloud-hosted servers: standard compute costs ($5-50/month for lightweight servers on VPS/containers), (3) Serverless: pay-per-invocation ($0.0001-0.001 per tool call typically), (4) Enterprise MCP gateways: vendor-specific pricing. The dominant cost in MCP-based systems is typically the LLM API usage, not the MCP infrastructure. A simple MCP server with a few tools can run on a $5/month VPS.
deployment_and_operations.resource_requirements: Extremely lightweight for the protocol itself. MCP servers are typically small processes: (1) Minimum: single-core CPU, 256MB RAM for a basic stdio server, (2) Kubernetes pod: 256Mi memory request, 500m CPU (typical), (3) Full deployment with monitoring: multi-core CPU, 16-32GB RAM, NVMe SSDs, 1Gbps network. Python 3.10+ or Node.js 18+ for SDK-based servers. No GPU required. Network connectivity required only for remote (Streamable HTTP) servers. The SDKs themselves have minimal dependencies.

observability_and_ops.monitoring_integration: Extensive ecosystem of observability tools: Datadog LLM Observability (end-to-end MCP client tracing), IBM Instana (MCP Observability module), Langfuse (open-source, mcp-use integration), Moesif (JSON-RPC payload analysis for MCP servers), SigNoz (OpenTelemetry-based MCP observability), Portkey (agent workflow debugging), Traceloop (MCP application testing), Prometheus + Grafana for infrastructure metrics. OpenTelemetry is a natural fit for MCP observability due to shared design philosophy and W3C Trace Context propagation.
observability_and_ops.tracing_support: Yes — MCP's JSON-RPC 2.0 foundation provides structured message traces by default. Request/response pairs are correlated via JSON-RPC IDs. OpenTelemetry context propagation works across MCP service boundaries. Dedicated MCP tracing available via Jaeger, Datadog, Langfuse, and other platforms. Every tool invocation, resource read, and notification is traceable. MCP gateways add centralized tracing and audit logging.
observability_and_ops.production_readiness_level: production_ready — MCP is deployed in production across the world's largest AI products: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, VS Code, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, and many more. Fortune 500 companies are running MCP in production including financial services institutions. The specification is mature (1 year old, multiple revisions, AAIF governance). However, the ecosystem is still evolving rapidly: the official registry is in preview, the MCP Apps Extension is new, and security concerns (tool redefinition attacks, prompt injection, over-privilege) are actively being addressed.

adoption_and_market.key_use_cases: Developer tooling (GitHub, GitLab, Jira, Linear integration for AI coding assistants). Enterprise data access (connecting LLMs to internal databases, CRMs, ERPs securely). Customer service automation (tool-equipped agents accessing business systems). Document intelligence and knowledge management. Financial services (fraud detection, compliance, trading data access). Healthcare (secure EMR orchestration). Retail/e-commerce (personalized AI shopping assistants). Manufacturing (predictive maintenance data pipelines). Legal tech (document management and analysis). Government (secure AI orchestration with audit trails).
adoption_and_market.competitive_position: Dominant market position — MCP has won the 'AI tool protocol' race. It is the de facto standard for connecting AI systems to external tools and data, with adoption from every major AI company. No serious competitor exists for the same problem space (agent-to-tool connectivity). Function calling (OpenAI-originated) is complementary but model-specific; MCP provides model-agnostic standardization. A2A (Google) is complementary, addressing agent-to-agent communication. ACP (Cisco/BeeAI) and ANP target similar but distinct niches with less traction. MCP's donation to the Linux Foundation via AAIF cemented its position as the neutral industry standard. The rare collaboration between Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft on MCP is unprecedented in AI.

human_agent_interaction.autonomy_spectrum: Not applicable as a protocol — MCP provides the infrastructure for any autonomy level. Tool annotations (read-only, destructive, open-world) enable clients to calibrate autonomy. Elicitation enables human-in-the-loop for sensitive decisions. The protocol supports the full spectrum from copilot to fully_delegated depending on client implementation.
human_agent_interaction.handoff_mechanism: MCP defines Elicitation as the mechanism for server-to-human communication: when a server needs human input (credentials, confirmations, complex decisions), it can redirect the user to a browser-based flow via URL mode Elicitation. The protocol also supports notifications from server to client for status updates. Actual human handoff in agent workflows is handled by the agent framework (not MCP), though MCP provides the tool/resource connectivity that agents use during handoffs.
human_agent_interaction.feedback_loop: Not directly implemented at protocol level. MCP enables feedback loops indirectly: (1) Resource subscriptions allow real-time data updates that reflect changed user preferences, (2) Tool invocations can write feedback to external systems, (3) The protocol's structured logging enables post-hoc analysis for improving tool descriptions and server behavior. The Hugging Face MCP Course covers feedback patterns. Actual feedback-to-improvement loops are implemented at the application/agent layer.

entrepreneurial_relevance.startup_applicability: Critical infrastructure knowledge for any AI startup. USE MCP WHEN: (1) Building an AI product that needs to connect to external tools/data — MCP is the standard, (2) Building a developer tool or SaaS and want AI integration — publish an MCP server so any AI assistant can use your product, (3) Need model-agnostic tool connectivity — avoid vendor lock-in to a single LLM provider, (4) Building agentic AI workflows that require real-world data access (databases, APIs, file systems), (5) Want to leverage the existing ecosystem of 8,000+ MCP servers rather than building custom integrations. AVOID/WAIT WHEN: (1) Building a simple chatbot with no external tool needs — MCP adds unnecessary complexity, (2) Only need basic RAG — direct vector store integration may be simpler than MCP, (3) Need agent-to-agent communication — use A2A protocol instead (MCP is agent-to-tool). STARTUP OPPORTUNITY: MCP creates a new market category for 'MCP-native' startups: MCP server hosting/management (CData, MintMCP), MCP security gateways (Stacklok, Solo.io, Pomerium), MCP registries/directories (PulseMCP, mcpservers.org), and MCP-first SaaS tools. 'Buy to learn, build to differentiate' — start with community MCP servers, build custom ones where you have domain expertise. Capital-efficient: a valuable MCP server can cost pennies to run but provide dollars of value per use.
entrepreneurial_relevance.build_vs_buy: The protocol and SDKs are free and open-source — no buy decision needed for the protocol itself. The key decision is: BUILD your own MCP servers for proprietary tools/data, or USE existing community/commercial MCP servers. BUILD when: you have unique data sources, need custom business logic, want to differentiate on integration quality. USE existing servers when: connecting to standard tools (GitHub, Slack, databases) — dozens of battle-tested servers already exist. For MCP infrastructure: BUY an MCP gateway (Stacklok, Solo.io) for enterprise security rather than building your own auth/audit layer. Cost comparison: building a basic MCP server takes 1-2 days of developer time; using an existing one takes minutes of configuration.
